messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] interpreting parametric bootstrapping plots
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jami,

I think your interpretation of the plot is correct. To get a p-value,
just type the name of the object that holds your results. Following
the example from the parboot help page, you would just type: pb.

If I understand your other question, you really want to compare
detection probabilities between biologists and volunteers. To do this
you could treat observer type as an observation-level covariate and
include it in the detection part of the model. To calculate detection
probs after 3 visits, you could backTransform the estimates for each
observer type and then use the formula 1 - (1 - p)^3. The expected
observed abundance would be this value times true abundance (under the
Poisson model).

Ian and I have talked about adding power analysis methods, but it's
not high on the list. Plus the N-mixture model isn't exactly designed
to model trends, so it might not be an appropriate use of pcount. If
you want to write your own code, you could do some simulations to
determine the number of sites and visits that would be necessary to
estimate abundance at some level of precision for each observer type.
Here's a bare minimum simulation:

nSites <- 20
nReps <- 3
lambda <- 10
p <- 0.5
y <- matrix(NA, nSites, nReps)
N <- rpois(nSites, lambda)
y[] <- rbinom(nSites*nReps, N, p) # Avoid for loop using R's recycling rules
y

Richard

Quoting Jami <octop...@yahoo.com>:

> I finally got my models running (thanks everyone for your help with
> this) and just ran 100 simulations using the parboot function.
>
> It looks the model fits.  This is how I'm interpreting the histogram.
> The observed residual variance, or root mean squared error (dashed
> vertical line) is within the distribution of the expected residual
> variance (bars in plot) and is just to the left of the bar with the
> highest frequency (is within the bar with the second highest
> frequency).  Is this a correct interpretation?
>
> I am not getting a p value on the plot as seen in the tutorial, nor an
> nsim= 100.   What is typically reported as the metric for goodness of
> fit here?
>
>
> On another note I am comparing volunteer estimates of mountain goat
> abundance to biologists estimates.  The biologists went to most sites
> 3 times each while the volunteers wnet to sites as many times as they
> could (up to 14 times).  To determine the effect of # of site visits I
> would like to do a simulation where I randomly pull 3 of the site
> visits at each site by volunteers to create a new dataset. And then do
> this 100 to 1000 times and generate an estimate of abundance/detection
> for each simulated dataset.    Any ideas for a way to  do this?
>
> Also wondering if you have any ideas for how I could do a power
> analysis to determine the differences in power between biologists and
> volunteers in their ability to detect a 30% decline in population
> size.
> Thanks,
> Jami
>
>

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: interpreting parametric bootstrapping plots
messages.body_plain:
exp(beta) = abundance
exp(beta +/- SE) = upper or lower SE
exp(beta +/- (SE*1.96)) = upper or lower 95% CI

exp(beta)/(1 + exp(beta)) = detectability
exp(beta +/- (SE*1.96))/(1 + exp(beta +/-(SE*1.96))) = detectability with U and L 95% CL's

I think.  if you're making predictions manually, don't forget to add covariate betas to the intercept beta before back-transforming.

Matt

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: interpreting parametric bootstrapping plots
messages.body_plain:
Those calculations for the coefficients (beta) and CI's are right.  That is, they are just back-transformed.  But for the standard errors, we use the delta method (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delta_method).  This basically multiples the backtranformed version of the variance by the derivative squared.

And don't forget that other methods are available for SE and confint -- you can also specify the method argument to either SE or confint:

fm <- nonparboot(fm, B = 100)
SE(fm, type = "det", method = "nonparboot")

and

confint(fm, type = "det", method = "profile")

Hope that helps,
Ian

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Predict using a colext object
messages.body_plain:
I will put that on the to-do list. In the meantime, note that predict
is basically just a convenience wrapper for linearComb. See
?linearComb for examples of getting predictions without predict. And
continuing with the colext example, you can do something like this:

# Logit-scale estimate of colonization prob in year 3
lc <- linearComb(fm.yearly, c(1,0,1,0,0,0), type="col")

# Back-transform it and get confidence interval

confint(backTransform(lc))

Richard

messages.body_plain:
Hi Richard,

Yep.  That did the trick.  Just need to update the package.  Thank you.
By the way, I have not played around with the colext function much.  But, is there a way of estimating conditional extinction probabilities between time periods?  By conditional, I mean making it conditional on the species actually occupying a site during the first time period.  Thank you.

Ben

-----Original Message-----
From: unma...@googlegroups.com [mailto:unma...@googlegroups.com] On Behalf Of rcha...@nrc.umass.edu
Sent: Thursday, May 13, 2010 1:37 PM
To: unma...@googlegroups.com
Subject: RE: [unmarked] Predict using a colext object

Hi Ben,

It works fine for me. What version of unmarked are you using? It
probably needs to be unmarked_0.8-6. To see, type:

sessionInfo()

In the new version you should see a slot named 'covMatBS' when you type:

slotNames(fm.yearly)

If that isn't the problem, type: traceback() after the error and let
me know what you get.

Richard

messages.body_plain:
Hi Stéphanie,

Without replicate surveys per site you cannot fit the Mackenzie model.
I will add a better error message for this case. The one model that
might work is the Royle et al 2004 distance sampling model, which can
be fit using the distsamp function. Did you record distances?

Richard
